questions.text: I treat my calendar as a binding contract with myself.
I experience the tension before a performance or presentation as an almost intolerable buildup of energy.
I ramp up effort as a project progresses, letting early stages stay loose and exploratory.
I prefer to keep my options open rather than lock myself into a specific course of action.
I rarely pick up on the nonverbal negotiation that happens before a group makes a decision.
I sequence my tasks so that each one builds logically on the one before.
I often need someone to explain the social dynamics of a situation after the fact.
The hardships of people I have no connection to carry little weight for me.
I think of my daily habits as investments that pay dividends in the years ahead.
I find it natural to defer my own interests when group needs arise.
I avoid detailed project timelines because they rarely survive contact with reality.
I enjoy shaping the culture of any team I join.
I routinely calculate the return on investment for my personal time and money.
I notice that my sleep quality is rarely affected by emotional events from the preceding day.
I tend to navigate most situations without noticeable shifts in my internal state.
I frequently take on captain or leadership roles in team settings.
I notice when someone's reply to a group message is really only intended for one person in the thread.
I prefer to control the narrative around a project's progress.
I rarely notice when a person carefully positions a negative opinion as a question to soften the delivery.
I gravitate toward letting discussions continue until the group is satisfied.
The felt weight of another person's suffering strongly motivates me to act for them.
I routinely write thoughtful, detailed feedback for others' projects even when no one asks.
I notice that even anticipating a difficult conversation makes my palms sweat and my heart race.
The suffering of people I don't know rarely seems important to me.
Even when someone I know is suffering deeply, I feel little concern about what happens to them.
I tend to choose careers and projects based on how much they allow me to help others.
I am usually the first to check in with the group before anyone takes charge.
When something excites me, the rush of energy is almost overwhelming.
I feel at home rotating representation duties among group members.
When an explanation shows me how someone is being harmed, I begin to care about what happens to them.
I feel that healthy self-focus gives me the strength to show up fully in everything I do.
I feel like I can sense what a group's unwritten rules are without being told.
I notice that my heart rate stays fairly constant even during heated discussions.
When someone is suffering, I want to act, not just understand.
I tend to think of my career as the central project of my life.
I can tell when someone is interested in a conversation topic versus enduring it out of courtesy.
